o: Choose a subset S of students such that every selected student i has |S| > nums[i] and every unselected student i has |S| < nums[i]. Only the size k of the selection matters (selections of the same size are interchangeable in validity): S is valid iff k > max(nums[i] for selected) and k < min(nums[i] for unselected). After sorting, k is achievable iff nums[k−1] < k (largest threshold among the k selected) and nums[k] > k (smallest threshold among the unselected). Example 1: [1,1] → k=0 (0<1 ok) and k=2 (2>1 ok) → 2 ways. Example 2 yields k ∈ {1,4,8}.
k: Validity depends only on selection size k, not which students.
After sorting, size k works iff nums[k-1] < k and nums[k] > k (with boundary conventions).
Count all such k in 0..n — O(n log n) with sorting, O(n) with counting sort.

a.n: Approach 1: Sort and Check Each Size
a.i: Sort nums. For each candidate size k from 0 to n, verify the selected block (the k smallest thresholds) and the unselected block conditions; count successes.
s: For k in 0..n: valid iff (k == 0 or nums[k-1] < k) and (k == n or nums[k] > k).
a.t: O(n log n) — sorting dominates; the scan is linear

w: Strict inequalities matter: selecting exactly nums[i] students makes student i unhappy. Always test k=0 (empty group valid iff all nums[i] > 0) and k=n (valid iff all nums[i] < n, guaranteed by constraints... actually nums[i] < n holds, so k=n is always valid — a good sanity check). Follow-up: count selections themselves (combinatorial), or handle students indifferent to selection.
